content: 1. In one study (den Boon, 2006), there was a high risk of selection bias, and in two studies, the risk of bias related to the reference standard was unclear. In nine out of eleven studies, fewer than half of the participants received the reference standard. Accuracy was calculated under the assumption that those who did not receive the reference standard were culture and/or smear negative, indicating no active tuberculosis (TB). 2. There were no major concerns regarding the applicability of the studies, as assessed using the QUADAS-2 tool. 3. Moderate heterogeneity was observed in sensitivity estimates, while significant heterogeneity was noted in specificity estimates based on visual inspection of confidence intervals (CIs). Specificity was downgraded due to this inconsistency. 4. Sensitivity estimates were precise, but specificity estimates were imprecise, leading to concerns about the reliability of specificity data. 5. Publication bias was not formally assessed due to the limited evidence base for evaluating publication bias in diagnostic test accuracy studies. However, it is expected to be likely. 6. The GRADE profile tables for new recommendations on latent tuberculosis infection (LTBI) management were updated and consolidated. These guidelines evaluated whether interferon-gamma release assays (IGRAs) could serve as an alternative to tuberculin skin tests (TSTs) for identifying individuals at high risk of progression from LTBI to active TB in high TB incidence settings. 7. Longitudinal studies on the predictive value of a positive IGRA in high TB incidence countries (≥100/100,000) are still emerging. These studies should ideally have an average follow-up of at least one year, which can be either active or passive. 8. The overall quality of evidence was assessed using the GRADE approach. All studies started with one point deducted because none were randomized controlled trials (RCTs). Quality assessments were based on relative effect measures (e.g., relative risk or incidence rate ratio) for both TST and IGRA. 9. Studies were not downgraded if both tests scored high on specific GRADE quality items. However, concerns such as selection bias, incorporation bias, ascertainment bias, and publication bias were considered when assessing the risk of bias. 10. Microbiological methods were used to ascertain TB in the studies, but not all incident TB cases had a definitive culture-confirmed diagnosis. Publication bias was not formally assessed but was expected to be likely. Several large prospective studies are ongoing or unpublished, and their results were not included in this analysis. 11. Serious unexplained inconsistency was noted in the relative risk estimates for TST, leading to downgrading. Similarly, serious imprecision in the relative risk estimates for TST was identified, as the lower limit of the 95% CI indicated a lack of predictive utility. 12. For IGRA and TST, pooled estimates were based on only two studies, one involving HIV-infected individuals on antiretroviral therapy (ART) with a median CD4+ count of approximately 250, and another involving HIV-infected antepartum and postpartum women. This limited evidence base contributed to concerns about imprecision and inconsistency. 13. Very serious imprecision was observed in the relative risk estimates for both TST and IGRA, with wide CIs indicating both significant predictive performance and a lack of predictive utility. The studies had few events, further contributing to imprecision. 14. In studies involving healthcare workers, selection bias, lack of microbiological tools for TB ascertainment, incorporation bias, and publication bias were identified as potential issues. Publication bias was not formally assessed but was expected to be likely. Results from ongoing or unpublished large prospective studies were not included in the analysis. 15. For adolescents in high TB incidence settings, no direct evidence was available for other subpopulations of children or adolescents. Serious imprecision was noted in TST effect estimates, with the lower limit of the 95% CI indicating a lack of predictive utility. 16. Preventive treatment options for LTBI in children and adolescents under 15 years of age were evaluated. A three-month daily regimen of rifampicin plus isoniazid (3RH) was compared to six or nine months of isoniazid monotherapy. The overall quality of evidence was low, with adherence rates and treatment outcomes being key considerations. 17. For adults with HIV, a three-month weekly regimen of rifapentine plus isoniazid (3HP) was compared to six or nine months of isoniazid monotherapy. The overall quality of evidence was high, with no downgrading for most quality domains. However, open-label trial designs may have introduced ascertainment bias. 18. For adults without HIV, the quality of evidence for 3HP versus isoniazid monotherapy was moderate. The studies showed no significant differences in outcomes, but the evidence was downgraded due to imprecision and concerns about the generalizability of findings. 19. Preventive treatment for contacts of patients with multidrug-resistant or rifampicin-resistant TB was assessed. The overall quality of evidence was very low, with small sample sizes, wide CIs, and a lack of adjustment for confounders contributing to the downgrading of evidence. 20. Mortality, adverse events, and the development of drug resistance were not adequately reported in the studies, making it impossible to estimate these outcomes. The lack of evidence highlights the need for further research in this area.
